caption:
Why was Tesla's Wardenclyffe Tower never finished?

In March 1901 J. P. Morgan signed a contract giving Nikola Tesla $150,000 to build a wireless station on Long Island that could send messages to London and to ships at sea. Morgan took a 51% interest in the company and in the patents.

Then Tesla changed the plan. After reading a June 1901 article by Marconi, he decided a small pilot plant would not impress investors, and scaled up to a much more powerful transmitter that would also carry telephony, images, and wireless power. He told Morgan in July 1901 that he needed much more money. Morgan refused and demanded an account of what had been spent.

The tower reached its full height of 187 feet by the end of 1902. Tesla's system did not use radio waves — he doubted Hertzian waves were useful and believed he could inject current into the ground at the right frequency and make the whole planet resonate. Under the tower he sank a shaft 120 feet deep and pushed sixteen iron pipes out 300 feet, in his words, "to have a grip on the earth so the whole of this globe can quiver."

It never became operational. On July 14, 1903, Morgan wrote that he would make no further advances. That night, and for several nights after, newspapers reported the tower shooting off bright flashes that lit up the sky. No explanation ever came from Tesla or his workers, and Wardenclyffe never seemed to operate again. When Tesla could not pay his hotel mortgages, the property was foreclosed and the tower was dynamited for scrap on July 4, 1917, realizing $1,750.

Still unresolved: what the flashes of July 1903 were, what the four 100-foot tunnels radiating from the base of the shaft were for, and how Tesla meant to combine ground conduction with his charged-atmosphere idea. Because his mortgages and foreclosure were kept off the public record, he could not publicly refute the wartime rumor that the government had ordered the tower destroyed.

Photographs: the plant at Wardenclyffe around 1902, a 1904 view made to show Morgan, the 1917 demolition attributed to the American Press Association, and Tesla's own patent drawing for US 1,119,732.

cards.headline: This tower <y>never went into operation</y>
cards.note: Wardenclyffe, Shoreham, New York. Built 1901–1902. Abandoned in 1906.
cards.alt: Skeletal wooden tower with flat top rising behind a long brick laboratory building.

cards.headline: The plan: <y>use the Earth as the wire</y>
cards.note: Tesla rejected radio waves. He theorized that current injected into the ground at the right frequency would make the planet resonate in standing waves that could be tapped anywhere — signals out through the earth, returning through the air.
cards.alt: Patent line drawing of a tall coil on a tripod mast with two ring-shaped terminals on top.

cards.headline: Morgan said no. <y>Tesla kept building.</y>
cards.note: Morgan's contract of March 1901 promised $150,000 and took 51% of the company and its patents. When Tesla enlarged the design and asked for more, Morgan refused. This 1904 photograph was made so Tesla could go back and ask again.
cards.alt: Sepia photograph of the completed lattice tower with domed cupola beside the brick plant.

cards.headline: A shaft <y>120 feet straight down</y>
cards.note: Tesla kept press and public away, so little is known. His 1923 testimony describes a wood and steel lined shaft sunk 120 feet under the tower, with sixteen iron pipes pushed out 300 feet — "to have a grip on the earth so the whole of this globe can quiver."
cards.alt: Detail of the tower's wooden legs meeting the roof and brick chimney of the plant below.

cards.headline: <y>Dynamited for scrap</y> on July 4, 1917
cards.note: The Smiley Steel Company of New York began demolition with dynamite. The first blast only knocked the tower onto a tilt; it was not fully down until September. The scrap realized $1,750. A wartime rumor said the government ordered it destroyed as a German spy post.
cards.alt: Halftone photograph of the tall timber tower leaning steeply after the dynamite blast.

cards.headline: The flashes over Shoreham <y>were never explained</y>
cards.note: The night Morgan finally refused more money — July 14, 1903 — and several nights after, newspapers reported the tower shooting off bright flashes that lit the sky. Tesla and his workers said nothing about it, and Wardenclyffe never seemed to operate again. Four 100-foot tunnels radiating from the base of the shaft are still argued over: drainage, access, or something to do with resonance and the water table.
cards.alt: Halftone photograph of the intact Wardenclyffe tower and its domed cupola against pale sky.
